title: The Messy Reality of Scale: Synthetic Data and Pre-Training — Marah Abdin & Robert McHardy, poolside

primary.label: Model Foundations & Behavior
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 89%).

domains.label: Coding Assistants
domains.rationale: Poolside's Laguna S model is explicitly built for agentic coding, evaluated on coding benchmarks (EvalPlus, BigCodeBench, SweepBench agentless multilingual), and the synthetic data pipeline targets code data scarcity. The talk's payoff is a coding-specialized model.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The synthetic data pipeline techniques (rephrasing, multi-stage generation, cross-domain porting) and pre-training reliability methods (replica hashing, numerical precision fixes, FP8 race condition detection) are broadly applicable ML engineering practices that extend beyond coding to any large-scale LLM training scenario.

summary: Marah Abdin and Robert McHardy from Poolside present their approach to scaling synthetic data generation and pre-training reliability for large language models. Poolside released two open-weight MoE models—Laguna M.1 (225B total / 23B active) and Laguna XS.2 (33B total / 3B active)—with a technical report, and preview a larger 118B total / 8B active model (Laguna S) for agentic coding. Marah details the synthetic data strategy: synthetic data complements organic data by extracting implicit rationale, planning, and structure, comprising 13% of the pre-training mix in a 6-trillion-token corpus. The pipeline architecture has six modular components (seeds, primary inputs, metadata, secondary inputs, generators, validators) and four shapes: rephrasing, multi-stage pipelines, cross-domain porting, and multi-turn agent roles. Hive, Poolside's orchestration infrastructure, enables configurable generation with agent queues, orchestrators that police outputs and dynamically change instructions, and supervisor oversight. Early quality-over-quantity focus caused non-optimal repetition that saturated models prematurely; rephrasing pipelines addressed this with consistently positive ablation results. Robert covers pre-training with a trust-nothing philosophy: model replica hash comparison across distributed data-parallel replicas crashes training on any mismatch, catching silent failures including broken GPUs. A BF16 accumulation in tensor parallel for the unembedding caused Laguna M.1 to stop converging around 50,000 steps as activations grew; moving accumulation to FP32 restored convergence—a scale-dependent numerical precision failure. FP8 training via kernels introduced a race condition causing illegal memory accesses, NaNs, and approximately 0.5% silent gradient corruption, invisible to hash checks since real training lacks redundant replicas. Laguna S scales to 118B total / 8B active parameters trained on 30 trillion tokens across 4,000 GPUs. Early base-model evals show Laguna S outperforming XS.2, M.1, GLM 4.5 Air, Qwen 360, and DeepSeek V4 Flash Max on coding benchmarks, with strong SweepBench agentless multilingual results, while trailing on MMLU Pro—acknowledged as a pluggable data gap. The key conclusion: the training recipe held and scaled.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a tightly coupled narrative about scaling foundation model training from 33B to 118B parameters. The SE concepts—pipeline architecture with six modular components, Hive orchestration, replica hashing, and the trust-nothing philosophy—provide the infrastructure and reliability scaffolding that makes large-scale training possible. The AI concepts—synthetic data composition, BF16/FP32 numerical precision, FP8 gradient corruption, MoE architecture, convergence behavior, and specialization trade-offs—describe the specific technical challenges that arise at scale and how they manifest in model behavior. Together they explain why naive scaling fails: silent hardware corruption, BF16 precision limits, and FP8 race conditions are invisible without active verification, while synthetic data quality and pipeline design determine whether the model converges to the right distribution. The talk's payoff—Laguna S scaling the recipe from 33B to 118B—demonstrates that systematic engineering of both data pipelines and training reliability is prerequisite to predictable model scaling. The task decomposition principle bridges both domains: it guides synthetic data pipeline design (break hard tasks into stages) and mirrors the engineering philosophy (verify each component because trust is not assumed at scale).
temporalContext: This talk was published on 2026-07-26, five days after Poolside released Laguna S 2.1 as open-weights on 2026-07-21. The talk previews this 118B total / 8B active MoE model and presents early base-model evaluations, functioning as a launch-period technical deep dive. The Laguna M.1 and XS.2 models were released on 2026-04-28, with the arXiv technical report published on 2026-05-26. Research for this synthesis was conducted as of 2026-08-21, approximately four weeks after the video's publication, by which time Laguna S 2.1 was publicly available on Hugging Face with model card, blog post, press release, and official documentation all confirmed as verified first-party sources. The talk predates the public release but coincides with the launch window, making it a primary source for understanding Poolside's engineering decisions.

concepts.name: Synthetic data generation for LLM pre-training
concepts.explanation: Synthetic data complements organic data by extracting implicit features—rationale, planning, structure—and projecting them onto new planes. It comprises 13% of the pre-training mix for XS.2 in a 6-trillion-token corpus, with organic data remaining the majority.
concepts.importance: Core technique for scaling training data quality and quantity beyond what organic data alone can provide; the 13% figure quantifies synthetic data's role in a real production system.

concepts.name: BF16 vs FP32 numerical precision in tensor parallel accumulation
concepts.explanation: BF16 accumulation in tensor parallel for the unembedding lacks sufficient precision at scale as activations grow; Laguna M.1 stopped converging around 50,000 steps. Moving the accumulation to FP32 restored convergence and reduced gradient norms.
concepts.importance: A scale-dependent numerical precision failure that silently stops convergence and is only diagnosable through loss curve and gradient norm analysis—a failure class that cannot be detected in small-scale experiments.

concepts.name: FP8 training race conditions and silent gradient corruption
concepts.explanation: FP8 training via kernels introduced a race condition causing illegal memory accesses, NaNs in gradients, and approximately 0.5% silent gradient corruption—values replaced by random numbers—invisible to replica hash checks since real training lacks redundant replicas.
concepts.importance: Reveals a fundamental blind spot in verification: race-condition-induced corruption is undetectable by replica hashing, highlighting that no single verification mechanism covers all failure modes at scale.

concepts.name: Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture
concepts.explanation: Laguna S uses a 118B total / 8B active parameter MoE architecture, scaling the recipe from 33B (XS.2) while keeping active parameters small for efficient inference.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that MoE enables scaling total parameters for capability while maintaining inference efficiency through sparse activation—a key architecture choice for agentic coding models.

concepts.name: Model convergence behavior at scale
concepts.explanation: Convergence can silently stall at scale due to numerical precision issues around 50,000 steps, with loss curves and gradient norms serving as primary diagnostic signals. The failure only manifests as activations grow beyond BF16 precision limits.
concepts.importance: Understanding convergence failure modes is essential for diagnosing and fixing training issues at scale, where each failed run costs significant compute.

concepts.name: Silent data corruption from hardware failures
concepts.explanation: Broken GPUs cause silent data corruption producing spiky loss curves and huge gradient norms under identical configurations, detectable only through active verification like replica hash comparison.
concepts.importance: Hardware failures at scale are common and their effects are invisible without active verification mechanisms, making reliability engineering inseparable from model training.

concepts.name: Token uniqueness and premature model saturation
concepts.explanation: Repeating high-quality data causes non-optimal repetition that saturates the model prematurely; rephrasing pipelines address the token-uniqueness problem with consistently positive ablation results.
concepts.importance: Over-focusing on quality without diversity degrades training; token diversity matters as much as data quality in pre-training.

concepts.name: Pre-training data composition (synthetic vs organic)
concepts.explanation: Synthetic data settled at 13% of the pre-training mix for XS.2 in a 6-trillion-token corpus; organic data remains the majority and synthetic data complements rather than replaces it. The guiding principle is extracting implicit features from existing data.
concepts.importance: The balance between synthetic and organic data is a key design decision affecting model quality, diversity, and training efficiency.

concepts.name: Agentic coding benchmarks and evaluation
concepts.explanation: Laguna S is evaluated on coding benchmarks including EvalPlus Code Bench, BigCodeBench, and SweepBench agentless multilingual, showing early base-model results outperforming GLM 4.5 Air, Qwen 360, and DeepSeek V4 Flash Max on coding tasks.
concepts.importance: Benchmark selection—especially SweepBench as a proxy for agentic performance during pre-training—reflects Poolside's deliberate specialization toward agentic coding.

concepts.name: Scale-dependent numerical precision failures
concepts.explanation: The BF16 accumulation failure only manifests at scale as activations grow, making it impossible to detect in small-scale experiments—a class of failure requiring full-scale testing to surface.
concepts.importance: Highlights that some training failure modes are inherently scale-dependent and cannot be predicted from smaller runs, challenging conventional incremental testing approaches.

concepts.name: Training recipe scaling from 33B to 118B
concepts.explanation: The training recipe—including data insights, numerical precision fixes, and reliability mechanisms—held as it scaled from 33B (XS.2) to 118B (Laguna S), incorporating all prior learnings into the larger model's training.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that systematic engineering of data and training reliability enables predictable scaling of foundation models, validating the methodology at each scale step.

concepts.name: Gradient norms as diagnostic signals
concepts.explanation: Gradient norms alongside loss curves serve as primary diagnostic signals: broken GPUs produce huge gradient norms, and BF16 precision issues show elevated gradient norms before convergence stops. Monitoring both is essential for early detection.
concepts.importance: Gradient monitoring complements loss curve analysis, revealing training failures that loss curves alone may not expose.

concepts.name: Task decomposition for synthetic data generation
concepts.explanation: If a synthetic data task is too hard for the model, it loses correctness and diversity; the guiding principle is to break it down into sub-tasks the model can handle. This determines the boundary between direct generation and multi-stage decomposition.
concepts.importance: Establishes the core decision rule for synthetic data pipeline design: model capability dictates pipeline complexity and decomposition strategy.

concepts.name: Model specialization trade-offs (agentic coding vs general knowledge)
concepts.explanation: Laguna S prioritizes agentic coding performance—leading on coding benchmarks—while trailing on MMLU Pro, a trade-off acknowledged as a pluggable data gap rather than an architectural limitation.
concepts.importance: Illustrates that foundation model specialization involves deliberate trade-offs in training data composition and evaluation, and that weaknesses can be addressed through data without architectural changes.

concepts.name: Model replica hash verification for distributed training
concepts.explanation: Comparing weight hashes across distributed data-parallel replicas and crashing training on any mismatch to detect silent failures including broken GPUs. Identical hashes mean continue; mismatch means crash the training run.
concepts.importance: Essential reliability mechanism for large-scale distributed training where silent hardware failures are otherwise undetectable and can corrupt weeks of compute.

concepts.name: Trust-nothing philosophy in distributed training
concepts.explanation: At training scale, no computation is trusted by default; every step is actively verified through mechanisms like replica hashing and crash-on-mismatch. The team explicitly states 'we don't trust anything.'
concepts.importance: Prevents silent corruption from compounding through expensive multi-week training runs, establishing a reliability-first engineering culture for frontier-scale training.

concepts.name: Hive multi-agent generation infrastructure
concepts.explanation: Poolside's configurable generation infrastructure with queues of agents (each having prompts, parameters, models, inputs, outputs), orchestrators that police generations and dynamically change instructions or choose which agent runs next, and a supervisor with global oversight.
concepts.importance: Enables scalable, quality-controlled synthetic data generation through coordinated multi-agent workflows, supporting the 13% synthetic data fraction in pre-training.

concepts.name: Synthetic data pipeline architecture (six modular components)
concepts.explanation: Six modular components—seeds, primary inputs, metadata, secondary inputs, generator functions, and validators—compose pipelines spanning from cheap seed-heavy small-model workflows to complex orchestrated multi-stage systems.
concepts.importance: Provides a reusable, composable framework for generating diverse training data at scale, allowing teams to trade cost against complexity based on the data gap being filled.

concepts.name: Rephrasing pipelines for data augmentation
concepts.explanation: Rephrasing high-quality data addresses token-uniqueness problems and premature model saturation caused by repeating the same high-quality content. Ablation results consistently show improvement from rephrased tokens versus repeated seed tokens.
concepts.importance: Solves the quality-over-quantity pitfall where repeated high-quality data saturates the model prematurely, making data diversity as important as data quality.

concepts.name: Multi-stage generation pipelines
concepts.explanation: Pipeline shape where complex outputs are built in stages—for example, generating setting, characters, and plot first, then writing chapters one by one—enabling decomposition of hard generation tasks into manageable sub-tasks.
concepts.importance: Allows generating complex structured content that would be infeasible in a single pass, directly applying the break-it-down principle when tasks exceed model capability.

concepts.name: Cross-domain data porting
concepts.explanation: Transforming data from one domain to another—for example, converting math problems to code—to fill data gaps and leverage existing high-quality data in new modalities without collecting new organic data.
concepts.importance: Expands the utility of curated datasets across modalities, addressing data scarcity in target domains by reusing high-quality sources from related domains.

concepts.name: Multi-turn agent role pipelines (judge-evolver)
concepts.explanation: Pipeline shape where agents iterate for k rounds (e.g., judge-evolver pipelines) generating multi-turn agent chats, with orchestrators policing quality and dynamically changing instructions between rounds.
concepts.importance: Enables iterative quality improvement through agent interaction, producing complex conversational training data through controlled multi-turn generation.

sections.title: Introduction: synthetic data and pre-training at poolside
sections.summary: Marah Abdin introduces herself and poolside, mentioning two open-weight models (Laguna M and Laguna XS) released on Hugging Face with a tech report. The transition from .1 to .2 involved many changes, and a newer model will be previewed.

sections.title: Why synthetic data
sections.summary: Marah explains three data-side improvements: auto mixer for cheaper sweeps, rethought web data sampling for higher recall, and more synthetic data. Synthetic data complements organic data by extracting implicit rationale, planning, and structure. Settled at 13% of pre-training mix for XS .2, with a 6-trillion-token corpus growing continuously.

sections.title: Limitations and the training budget
sections.summary: Early quality-over-quantity focus led to non-optimal repetition of high-quality data, saturating the model prematurely. Rephrasing addressed the token-uniqueness problem, with ablation results consistently showing improvement. Beyond generic rephrasing, specialized pipelines were built for STEM documents and code-text conversion.

sections.title: Inside the synthetic data pipeline
sections.summary: Marah describes six modular pipeline components: seeds, primary inputs, metadata, secondary inputs, generator functions, and supplementary functions. Pipelines span an axis from cheap seed-heavy small-model pipelines to complex orchestrated workflows. Rule of thumb: if a task is too hard for the model, break it down to avoid losing correctness and diversity.

sections.title: Multistage pipelines and porting data
sections.summary: Four shapes of synthetic data are presented: rephrasing, multi-stage pipelines (e.g., novel generation by first building setting, characters, plot, then chapters), cross-domain porting (e.g., math problems to code), and multi-turn roles (e.g., agent chats, judge-evolver pipelines iterating for k rounds).

sections.title: Multi-turn chats and policing generations
sections.summary: Marah introduces Hive, poolside's configurable generation infrastructure with queues of agents (each with prompts, parameters, models, inputs, outputs), orchestrators that police generations and dynamically change instructions or choose which agent runs next, and a supervisor with global oversight.

sections.title: Pre-training: trust nothing, crash on mismatch
sections.summary: Robert McHardy covers architecture and distributed training. The team trusts nothing at scale. They use model replica hashes—calculating weight hashes across distributed data parallel replicas and periodically comparing them. Identical hashes mean continue; mismatch means crash the training.

sections.title: Failures at scale: broken GPUs
sections.summary: Robert shares a broken GPU example: two loss curves under identical configuration, one spiky with huge gradient norms due to a broken GPU causing silent data corruption. This was detectable via replica hash comparison since the computation should have been identical across replicas.

sections.title: Numerical precision and corrupted gradients
sections.summary: Robert details a BF16 precision failure: Laguna M 1 stopped converging around 50,000 steps because activations grew before the LM head and the tensor-parallel accumulation for the unembedding was performed in BF16, lacking sufficient precision. Moving accumulation to FP32 restored convergence and reduced gradient norms. This failure only manifests at scale. XGen-2 (XS .2) at 33B parameters is open-weights and competitive for coding. Laguna S previews at 118B total / 8B active parameters, trained on 30 trillion tokens across 4,000 GPUs.

sections.title: A 118B model for agentic coding
sections.summary: Laguna S scales the recipe to 118B total / 8B active parameters on 30 trillion tokens across 4,000 GPUs. FP8 training using DeepChem kernels introduced a race condition causing illegal memory accesses, NaNs in gradients, and ~0.5% silent gradient corruption—replaced by random values. This is a blind spot in hash checks since real training runs lack redundant replicas with identical weights and data. A fix is available in a public PR not yet merged into DeepChem.

sections.title: Early results vs GLM 4.5 Air
sections.summary: Robert shares base-model evals (caveated as partly indicative). Laguna S outperforms XS .2, M.1, GLM 4.5 Air, Qwen 360, and DeepSeek V4 Flash Max on coding benchmarks (EvalPlus Code Bench, BigCodeBench). It is competitive on BigBench Hard and Eval Plus. It performs best on SweepBench agentless multilingual, used as a proxy for agentic performance during pre-training. It trails on MMLU Pro, acknowledged as a data gap rather than architectural limitation. The recipe held and scaled; Laguna S will be released as open-weights.

organization.name: Poolside, Inc.
organization.summary: Poolside, Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered at 548 Market St., PMB 53385, San Francisco, CA 94104, USA, founded in April 2023 in San Francisco by co-CEOs and co-founders Jason Warner (ex-CTO of GitHub) and Eiso Kant. The company self-describes as a frontier AI lab building its own foundation models to achieve AGI, with coding as its first major capability. Poolside builds open-weight MoE foundation models (the Laguna family: XS.2 at 33B/3B, M.1 at 225B/23B, S 2.1 at 118B/8B) and the Model Factory, an internal platform for versioned data, training, evaluation, and inference. The Applied Research organization comprises approximately 60 people across infrastructure, architecture, data, pre-training, and reinforcement learning. Poolside has raised $626M total funding, including a $500M Series B in October 2024 at a $3B valuation led by Bain Capital Ventures with participation from Nvidia, DST Global, StepStone Group, Citi Ventures, and HSBC Ventures.
organization.status: Active; Laguna S 2.1 released as open-weights on July 21, 2026 under OpenMDW-1.1 license; Laguna XS.2 and M.1 released April 28, 2026 under Apache 2.0

technologies.label: Laguna MoE Model Family
technologies.summary: Poolside's Laguna model family is a series of open-weight Mixture-of-Experts models designed for agentic coding, spanning from 33B total / 3B active (XS.2) to 225B total / 23B active (M.1) to 118B total / 8B active (S 2.1). The architecture features token-choice routing with softplus gating, shared experts alongside routed experts, grouped-query attention, and interleaved full/sliding-window attention. Laguna S 2.1, the largest model previewed in the talk, was trained on 30 trillion tokens across 4,000 GPUs and shows early base-model evals outperforming GLM 4.5 Air and other competitors on coding benchmarks while trailing on MMLU Pro. The Hugging Face Transformers library has official support for the Laguna architecture, confirming it as a recognized model family in the open-source ecosystem.
technologies.role: Central subject of the talk; all discussions of synthetic data, pre-training reliability, numerical precision, and evaluation culminate in the Laguna model family. The talk previews Laguna S 2.1 before its public release and presents early benchmark results.

technologies.label: Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline Architecture
technologies.primary: Synthetic Data Pipeline with Six Modular Components
technologies.summary: Poolside's synthetic data pipeline architecture comprises six modular components—seeds, primary inputs, metadata, secondary inputs, generator functions, and validators—spanning an axis from cheap seed-heavy small-model pipelines to complex orchestrated workflows. The guiding principle is: if a task is too hard for the model, break it down to avoid losing correctness and diversity. Four pipeline shapes are presented: rephrasing (addressing token-uniqueness and premature saturation), multi-stage pipelines (decomposing hard tasks into stages), cross-domain porting (transforming data across modalities), and multi-turn agent roles (iterative judge-evolver pipelines). Hive provides the orchestration infrastructure with agent queues, policing orchestrators, and supervisor oversight. Synthetic data comprises 13% of the pre-training mix for XS.2 in a 6-trillion-token corpus, complementing rather than replacing organic data by extracting implicit features—rationale, planning, and structure—from existing data.
technologies.role: First half of the talk (Marah Abdin's section) is entirely dedicated to synthetic data pipeline design, the six modular components, four pipeline shapes, and Hive orchestration infrastructure.

technologies.label: Distributed Training Reliability: Model Replica Hash Verification
technologies.primary: Model Replica Hash Verification with Crash-on-Mismatch
technologies.summary: Poolside's trust-nothing approach to distributed training reliability uses model replica hash verification: weight hashes are calculated across distributed data-parallel replicas and periodically compared. Identical hashes mean training continues; any mismatch crashes the training run. This technique catches silent failures including broken GPUs that cause silent data corruption—detectable because DDP replicas should produce identical computation. However, the technique has a known blind spot: race-condition-induced corruption (such as from FP8 kernels) is invisible to hash checks because real training lacks redundant replicas with identical weights and data. Gradient norm monitoring serves as a complementary diagnostic signal.
technologies.role: Opens Robert McHardy's pre-training section as the foundational reliability philosophy; the broken GPU example demonstrates its value and the FP8 race condition demonstrates its limitations.

technologies.label: Numerical Precision Management in Large-Scale Training
technologies.primary: BF16-to-FP32 Accumulation Fix in Tensor Parallel
technologies.summary: At training scale, numerical precision choices become critical failure points that are invisible in small-scale experiments. Two specific failures are detailed: (1) BF16 accumulation in tensor parallel for the unembedding lacks sufficient precision as activations grow, silently stopping convergence around 50,000 steps during Laguna M.1 training; moving the accumulation to FP32 restored convergence and reduced gradient norms. (2) FP8 training via kernels introduced a race condition causing illegal memory accesses, NaNs in gradients, and approximately 0.5% silent gradient corruption—values replaced by random numbers—invisible to replica hash checks since real training lacks redundant replicas with identical weights and data. Both failures are scale-dependent and represent a class of issues that cannot be predicted from smaller runs, challenging conventional incremental testing approaches. A fix for the FP8 race condition was mentioned as available in a public PR not yet merged into the kernel library.
technologies.role: Central to Robert McHardy's pre-training section; the BF16/FP32 fix and FP8 race condition are presented as key engineering discoveries that enabled successful scaling from 33B to 118B parameters.
